claims.text: Optimized heat treatment can induce a controlled level of lattice distortion in lightweight HEAs.
Optimized heat treatment can limit nanoscale phase segregation in lightweight HEAs.

Heat-treatment-controlled lattice distortion and limited phase segregation enable lightweight HEAs to combine low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The baseline lightweight HEA has moderate lattice distortion.
The baseline lightweight HEA has inherent nanoscale phase segregation.
Lattice distortion increases mechanical strength by enhancing dislocation pinning.
A controlled, limited degree of nanoscale phase segregation promotes formation of a uniform passive oxide film.
Maintaining chemical homogeneity promotes formation of a robust, uniform passive oxide layer.
The robust, uniform passive oxide layer protects the alloy against both aqueous corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Excessive phase segregation diminishes strengthening and passive-oxide benefits.
Optimized heat-treated samples will have higher compressive strength than the conventionally processed baseline.
Optimized heat-treated samples will have lower corrosion current density and/or improved passivity relative to the baseline.
Optimized heat-treated samples will form a more stable and adherent oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation than the baseline.
Overly aggressive heat treatment that causes excessive phase segregation will reduce mechanical, corrosion, and oxidation performance.
The strengthening mechanism ceases to operate when lattice distortion is insufficient to enhance dislocation pinning.
The proposed combined-property mechanism ceases to operate when phase segregation becomes sufficient to degrade mechanical properties and passive-oxide formation.
Diffusion kinetics and local compositional variations may contribute to the observed property changes.
Failure of the optimized treatment to produce statistically significant improvements in all three performance categories relative to both controls would falsify the hypothesis.
